strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: end-to-end reinforcement learning for LLM-based multi-agent systems, with a critic-free alternative to MAPPO.
The proposed MHGPO method is clearly described, with pseudo-code, three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR), and a concrete reward propagation mechanism.
The paper adapts group-relative advantage estimation from GRPO to multi-agent heterogeneous groups, which is a reasonable and practically motivated direction.
Experiments cover three standard multi-hop QA datasets (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue) and include useful analyses of validation curves, reward curves, agent output patterns, and a case study.
Efficiency motivation is practically relevant: removing the critic substantially reduces GPU memory usage, as shown for the MHGPO variants.
The appendix provides detailed prompts, hyperparameters, and algorithm listings, which helps partially with reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim that MHGPO consistently outperforms MAPPO is not supported by the results: MHGPO-IS underperforms MAPPO on all three datasets, and RR is not consistently better (e.g., on MuSiQue Acc/EM). The gains of FoF/RR over MAPPO are modest and lack statistical significance or multiple-seed variance estimates.

The evaluation protocol is problematic: validation is performed on the first 500 samples from the test set, which contaminates model selection and undermines the reported test results. A proper development set should be used.

The efficiency claims are unclear and potentially contradictory. While GPU memory savings are evident, Figure 6 appears to show PPO may have lower average time per step than some MHGPO variants, contrary to the text's claim that MHGPO training time remains lower than PPO.
Generalization is not demonstrated. The method is tested only on a three-agent search MAS with Llama3.1-8B, despite claiming applicability to general multi-agent systems and other agent types.

Baselines are weak and incomplete. Only MAPPO is trained as a MARL baseline; there is no comparison to naive per-agent GRPO/DAPO, other critic-free MARL methods, strong prompt-optimized/SFT MAS baselines, or LLM-judge/human evaluation.

Key design choices are not ablated: group size G, reward aggregation operator, reward propagation scheme, group identifier assignment, top-n sampling, KL penalty coefficient, and rollout strategy hyperparameters. Sensitivity and scaling behavior remain unknown.

Novelty is incremental: adapting GRPO-style group-relative advantages to multi-agent rollouts is a natural extension, and the claim of being the first systematic investigation of group-based optimization for MAS is overstated given prior work on MARL for LLM agents such as MARFT.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, MAPPO training details (critic architecture, GAE parameters, value loss) are incomplete, and results appear to be single runs without error bars or significance testing.

The heterogeneous group advantage estimation is heuristic and lacks theoretical analysis or convergence guarantees; grouping rollouts with different prompts/inputs may introduce bias that is not discussed.
The reward design is largely task-specific and heuristic, with no analysis of how robust the approach is to different reward functions or MAS configurations.
The 'without warm-up' claim is not clearly meaningful because all compared methods, including MAPPO, are trained without SFT warm-up in the experiments.

strengths: The paper tackles a real and well-motivated problem: the critic network in MAPPO-style multi-agent RL for LLM systems is memory- and compute-heavy and unstable across heterogeneous agent roles. The proposed critic-free, group-relative alternative is a sensible direction, and the paper quantifies the practical payoff (Figure 6: ~82% GPU memory for PPO vs. ~47–58% for MHGPO variants).

The presentation is generally clear and self-contained. The three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) are formalized, illustrated (Figures 3–4, 7), and backed by full pseudo-code in the appendix, and the agent prompts, reward design, and hyperparameters (Table 2) are documented.

The experimental section goes beyond a single leaderboard: it reports memory/time costs, training dynamics (Figures 5, 11, 12), intra-group similarity evolution (Figure 9), and a qualitative case study (Figure 10) showing how the Rewriter adapts its query style to the retriever over training.
Evaluation spans three datasets (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue), including out-of-domain settings, which is more than many comparable papers do.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is overstated and partly contradicted by the paper's own table. The abstract and conclusion assert that MHGPO "consistently outperforms MAPPO," but MHGPO-IS is worse than MAPPO on all three datasets (HotpotQA F1 45.58 vs. 46.40; 2Wiki 38.05 vs. 38.72; MuSiQue 18.42 vs. 19.74), and MHGPO-RR's MuSiQue EM (9.350) is identical to MAPPO's. Only FoF/RR show gains, and those gains are small (e.g., HotpotQA F1 49.4–49.7 vs. 46.4).

Statistical rigor is insufficient for the claims made. All results appear to come from a single RL training run with no seeds, no error bars, and no significance testing, despite RL fine-tuning being notoriously high-variance. Differences of 2–3 F1 points on a single run cannot support "consistently outperforms," and the IS-vs-MAPPO reversal suggests the reported ordering may be within noise.

Novelty is incremental and not clearly positioned against the closest prior work. The method is essentially GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) plus reward backpropagation applied to a three-agent pipeline. The related-work section itself cites MARFT (Liao et al., 2025b) as "a reinforcement learning framework specifically designed for MAS, enabling end-to-end optimization across interacting agents," yet MARFT is never compared against, nor is the difference from it articulated. The claim of being "the first systematic investigation of GOAs applied to MAS" is therefore weakly supported.

The evidence base is too narrow for the generality claimed. Everything is demonstrated on one backbone (Llama3.1-8B), one MAS instantiation (the three-agent search system of Chen et al., 2025), one epoch of online RL, and one training dataset. The paper repeatedly asserts the approach "applies to all MAS" and "is capable of being generalized to general MAS," but no such generalization is tested; even the stated focus (MASS) is a single system design.

Baselines are missing or apparently unfair. There is no comparison to the underlying Chen et al. (2025) method or to MARFT. The "Single LLM + RL" row reports EM 0.5 on HotpotQA, which strongly suggests a broken or mismatched output format rather than a genuine baseline, and the unoptimized MAS is worse than a single LLM (F1 22.8 vs. 22.8; Acc 20.8 vs. 21.3), which directly undercuts the paper's motivation that MAS is the promising architecture.

No component ablations. The MAPPO comparison conflates at least three differences (critic vs. group-relative baseline, sampling strategy, reward shaping/backpropagation), so it is impossible to attribute the observed gains. There is no ablation on group size G, on the aggregation operator in Eq. 4, on the reward backpropagation itself, or on the F1-based reward and format penalties, which are heuristic and unexamined.

Some analytical claims are asserted rather than demonstrated. The observation that "heterogeneous groups naturally evolve into homogeneous ones" (Figures 7 and 9) is drawn from a single run and a single example; the mechanistic explanation for why RR outperforms FoF is speculative and not validated (e.g., no controlled experiment isolating intra-group diversity).

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: end-to-end reinforcement learning for LLM-based multi-agent systems, with a critic-free approach to reduce instability and computational overhead.

Proposes MHGPO, a clear and plausible extension of GRPO to multi-agent settings, including heterogeneous group advantage estimation, reward backpropagation, and three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) with detailed algorithms.

Provides empirical evidence on three multi-hop QA datasets (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue) showing that MHGPO variants, especially FoF and RR, generally outperform MAPPO and unoptimized baselines; also reports memory and efficiency benefits.
The paper is generally well organized and includes useful implementation details, prompts, and algorithmic descriptions that aid understanding.
The study is relevant to computational linguistics and NLP, particularly for retrieval-augmented QA and multi-agent LLM systems.
weaknesses: Empirical scope is limited: only one LLM backbone (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct), one three-agent search MAS, and one training dataset (HotpotQA); no multi-seed runs, variance estimates, or statistical significance tests.

Reproducibility is not fully established: no code or artifact release is mentioned, and the use of the first 500 test-set samples as a validation set during training raises concerns about test-set leakage or implicit model selection.

Key design choices are not ablated: group size, sampling probabilities in RR, reward aggregation, reward propagation, and the effect of the agent-specific penalty terms are not systematically studied.

The claim that MHGPO 'consistently outperforms' MAPPO is overstated: on some datasets/metrics (e.g., MuSiQue accuracy/EM for MHGPO-RR, 2Wiki EM for MHGPO-FoF) the gains are marginal or slightly negative.

Methodological novelty is incremental: the work adapts GRPO to multi-agent settings via group identifiers and reward backpropagation, while related MARL-for-LLM methods already exist; the claimed 'first systematic investigation' is not fully substantiated.
Generalization to general MAS is asserted but not empirically demonstrated; all experiments are on the specific MASS architecture.
Theoretical insight is limited: the argument that heterogeneous groups naturally evolve into homogeneous ones is an empirical observation without formal analysis.

strengths: Addresses a timely and relevant problem: end-to-end reinforcement learning for LLM-driven multi-agent search systems, where prompt engineering and SFT are costly and brittle.
Proposes MHGPO, a critic-free group-based RL method with backward reward propagation and heterogeneous-group advantage estimation, and explores three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR).

Provides a fairly extensive empirical study: three multi-hop QA datasets, ablations on role-wise training, reward aggregation, reward design, group size, and analyses of training dynamics, GPU memory, time, and case studies.
Includes a theoretical formalization connecting MHGPO to single-context GRPO under idealized assumptions, with proofs and a constructed transcript equivalence.
Provides prompts, hyperparameters, and algorithm listings in the appendix, which supports reproducibility if the method description is clarified.
Reports consistent improvements over MAPPO, single-context PPO/GRPO, and RAG baselines on HotpotQA and OOD datasets, with notable efficiency gains over MAPPO.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method is essentially an adaptation of GRPO to multi-agent rollouts with heuristic reward propagation and grouping; the theoretical results are largely definitional/idealized and do not establish new optimization or convergence guarantees.

The method description is ambiguous and contains apparent inconsistencies. Algorithm 5 assigns group identifiers by trajectory index rather than by forking-agent/role as the text claims, making the grouping mechanism unclear and undermining reproducibility. Equation 4 and the backward reward aggregation are also underspecified (direct successor vs. all successors; averaging over what exactly).

The key theoretical assumption A3 (context sufficiency) is strong and often violated in practice. The claimed equivalence to single-context GRPO therefore only holds in an idealized regime, and the paper does not formally justify why heterogeneous grouping should improve optimization when A3 is relaxed.

Empirical gains are modest (e.g., roughly 2-3 F1 points over R1-Searcher) and main results lack error bars or statistical significance tests. Different variants win on different datasets (FoF(os) is often best but not highlighted as the main method; RR is chosen despite not being best on OOD or HotpotQA F1), weakening the central claim of consistent superiority.

Baseline fairness is questionable: MAPPO uses an 8B LLM critic, which is unusually heavy and may artificially depress its performance; PPO/GRPO baselines are single-context and not directly comparable to the multi-agent setting. No standard multi-agent GRPO with per-agent homogeneous groups is included beyond IS, whose definition and implementation are unclear.

The reward design is heavily hand-crafted (format penalties, terminal reward averaging) without ablation of the propagation scheme or credit assignment; agent-specific penalties and their coefficients are not tuned or analyzed.

Evaluation details are incomplete: retrieval corpus/preprocessing, the nonstandard token-level 'Accuracy' metric, the 'normalized answer-hit' EM, and statistical reliability are insufficiently described.
The paper overclaims novelty ('first systematic study,' 'first connection,' 'near-aligned per-token advantage') relative to the idealized and largely definitional theoretical contribution.

strengths: Introduces MHGPO, a critic-free group-based RL framework for multi-agent search systems, extending GRPO to multi-context MASS with heterogeneous group advantage estimation and backward reward propagation.
Proposes and analyzes three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) and characterizes their efficiency–effectiveness trade-offs.
Provides a theoretical bridge showing token-level equivalence to single-context GRPO under assumptions A1–A3, adding conceptual grounding beyond pure empirics.

Conducts extensive experiments on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue with Llama3.1-8B, including comparisons to MAPPO, PPO, GRPO, Search-o1, and R1-Searcher, plus ablations on role-wise training, reward aggregation, and group size.
Demonstrates substantial memory and compute savings over MAPPO, and provides training dynamics, case study, and progressive homogenization analysis.
Writing is clear and the appendix provides detailed algorithms, prompts, hyperparameters, and implementation details, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Main test results (Table 1) lack variance estimates or significance tests; only some ablations average over three seeds, making the consistency of reported gains harder to assess.

The theoretical equivalence relies on strong Assumption A3 (context sufficiency), which the paper acknowledges is relaxed in realistic MASS settings; no formal variance/stability analysis is provided for heterogeneous grouping under incomplete local contexts.
Empirical scope is limited: three agents, up to 8B parameters, static retrieval, and QA-only tasks; generalization to larger models, dynamic environments, and other agent topologies is untested.
HAPPO and other multi-agent RL baselines mentioned in related work are not empirically compared, leaving the relative merit of MHGPO among MARL methods less clear.
The RR strategy depends on fork probabilities and group-reassignment choices, but only one setting (0.7,0.1,0.2) is evaluated; sensitivity to these hyperparameters is not explored.
No code or artifact release is mentioned; reproducibility depends on the appendix, and some reward design choices (e.g., F1 terminal reward, format penalties) may be brittle or gameable.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and timely problem: end-to-end optimization of LLM-driven multi-agent search systems, moving beyond prompt engineering/SFT and critic-based MARL.

It proposes MHGPO, a critic-free group-based RL framework with backward reward propagation and heterogeneous-group advantage estimation, and shows that parameter sharing substantially reduces memory and compute overhead.
It systematically introduces and compares three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR), with ablation and efficiency analyses that clarify their trade-offs.
It provides a theoretical bridge to single-context GRPO under explicit assumptions, helping explain when heterogeneous grouping aligns with GRPO and when it exploits cross-context dependencies.
Experiments on HotpotQA and OOD 2WikiMultihopQA/MuSiQue show consistent gains over MAPPO and strong single-context RAG/RL baselines, with better GPU memory/time trade-offs.
Ablations on role-wise training, aggregation operators, reward design, and group size provide useful evidence for the design choices.
The limitations section is candid about task scope, model scale, agent count, and theoretical characterization.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees rely on strong assumptions (deterministic prompt construction and context sufficiency) that are often violated in practice; no variance or convergence analysis is provided for the practical heterogeneous-grouping regime.

The experimental scope is limited: training is only on HotpotQA, with a single 8B backbone and a fixed three-agent pipeline; scalability to larger models, more agents, and broader task types remains untested.
Main results in Table 1 appear to lack error bars or statistical significance testing over multiple random seeds, making the claim of consistent superiority less robust than it could be.
Novelty is moderate: MHGPO combines existing ideas (GRPO, parameter sharing, reward propagation), and the algorithmic advance over prior multi-agent RL/GRPO adaptations may be incremental.
No code or artifact link is provided, which limits reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameters and prompts in the appendix.
Comparison to other MARL baselines (e.g., HAPPO) is absent, and details of baseline tuning/training fairness (e.g., R1-Searcher/Search-o1 training on exactly the same data) are not fully specified.
The claim of being the first systematic study of group-based optimization algorithms for multi-agent search systems may be overstated given concurrent/related work such as MARFT.
